transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I get stuck doing the same checks and routines over and over until I can’t finish anything, even when I know it makes no sense. It's just incredibly exhausting, and it feels like it's completely taking over my life.
Do these repeated checks and routines happen because unwanted thoughts or fears keep coming into your mind, and does doing them temporarily reduce your anxiety?

Yes, exactly. My mind gets flooded with terrifying thoughts, like a house I worked on catching fire or a deck collapsing because I missed some tiny detail. To stop that awful feeling, I have to check the stove, locks, and power tools over and over, which is the only way I can get any temporary relief.

When these thoughts and checking rituals happen, do you recognize that they are excessive or unreasonable, or do they feel completely true and justified to you? Has that level of certainty changed over time?

I definitely recognize that it makes no sense and that I've already checked things ten times, but I still get gripped by this overwhelming dread that if I don't do it, something terrible will be my fault. I'm not really sure if that certainty has changed over time, but it has always felt like a constant, exhausting battle between my rational mind and the urge to check.

Do you also have any repetitive movements or sounds you feel driven to do, like blinking, shoulder jerking, throat clearing, or grunting? If so, did those start before or around the same time as the checking rituals?

No, I don't experience any of those kinds of repetitive movements or sounds like blinking, shoulder jerking, or throat clearing. My repetitive behaviors are strictly limited to the checking rituals I described.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes classic obsessive-compulsive symptoms: recurrent intrusive and unwanted thoughts about causing harm through missed details, preserved insight that these fears and rituals are unreasonable, and compulsive checking behaviors performed repeatedly to reduce anxiety. No tic symptoms were reported. The presentation is most consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder.
